title: Investigation of exercise-mimetic bioactive molecules as modulators of MMP activity and expression in cancer cells
journal: Journal of Enzyme Inhibition and Medicinal Chemistry

sections.abstract: Matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs), particularly MMP-2 and MMP-9, are directly involved in the degradation of the extracellular matrix preceding uncontrolled cancer growth and metastasis. For these reasons, MMPs are considered key therapeutic targets in the development of cancer treatments. Acknowledged for its prophylactic effects against various diseases including cancer, physical exercise has been reported to boost the immune system, enhance endogenous defence mechanisms, manage oxidative stress, and regulate MMP. Despite its benefits, patients with compromised capacity for physical activity due to injuries and frailty are often unable to take advantage of them. As a possible solution for this problem, the alternative therapeutic approach of exercise mimetics has been gaining traction through pharmacological interventions. Exercise mimetics are pharmacological agents that partially mimic the molecular and physiological benefits of physical exercise without requiring actual physical activity. Recent studies have indicated that the potential of these compounds may serve as candidates for further investigation in cancer treatment. In this study, the possible anti-cancer and anti-metastatic–related effects of six selected exercise mimetics ( i.e ., AICAR , Icariin , Berberine , Betaine , GW501516 , and Metformin ) were investigated by targeting activity and/or expression of MMP-2/9 in in vitro model. These compounds (i) inhibited MMP-2 activity by interacting with the active site and/or allosteric sites, (ii) downregulated MMP-2/9 expression by influencing STAT3 signalling pathways, and (iii) reduced lung cancer cells (A549) viability to varying degrees. Among the exercise mimetics, Icariin and Berberine have relatively stronger effects on both the activity of MMP-2 and the expression of MMP-2/9 in cancer cells. These findings highlight the novel potential of exercise mimetics as targeted cancer therapeutics through the regulation of MMP activity and expression in cancer progression and metastasis.
sections.introduction:
Cancer is a complicated and highly variable disease, characterised by the uncontrolled proliferation of cells, leading to tumour formation and metastasis 1 , 2 . Its complex pathophysiology involves numerous genetic mutations, dysregulation of oncogenes and tumour suppressor genes, and disruption of cellular signalling pathways 3 , 4 . Metastasis, the process by which cancer cells invade surrounding tissues and spread to distant organs, is responsible for approximately 90% of cancer-related deaths 5–7 . Despite advances in cancer therapies like chemotherapy, radiation, and immunotherapy, metastasis remains a major challenge, largely due to the resistance of metastatic cancer cells to current treatments 8 , 9 . While these approaches have also improved survival rates for certain cancers, they often come with significant limitations in advanced stages and metastasis, leading to poor patient outcomes 10 , 11 . For this reason, exploring alternative treatment options and the goal of developing more effective cancer treatments with fewer side effects remains a primary focus of current research.

Proteolytic enzymes, particularly matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs), are important proteases that cleave various components during the remodelling of the extracellular matrix (ECM), facilitating tumour invasion and metastasis 12 , 13 . They are closely involved in cancer progression by promoting tumour growth and dissemination 14 . Besides, their involvement in angiogenesis ensures a steady supply of nutrients and oxygen to the growing tumours 15 . This study focuses on MMP-2 (gelatinase A, 72 kDa) and MMP-9 (gelatinase B, 92 kDa) based on direct involvement in ECM remodelling, tumour cell invasion, and angiogenesis 16 , 17 . These two gelatinases are also implicated in the activation of growth factors, such as transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β), and modulating cell signalling pathways that influence tumour proliferation, apoptosis resistance, and immune evasion 18 , 19 . Research indicates a strong negative correlation between the overexpression of MMPs and survival rates in solid tumour patients 20–22 . MMP-9, in particular, has been closely linked to adverse prognoses in several malignancies, including breast, lung, colon, gastric, pancreatic, and prostate cancers. 23–26 Therefore, MMP-2/9 have been proposed as potential diagnostic and prognostic biomarkers in several types of cancer. 27 Despite limited results from early clinical trials about the development of MMP inhibitors, targeting MMPs remains a promising strategy to inhibit tumour invasion and angiogenesis, as well as improve cancer therapies, addressing current treatment limitations 28 , 29 .

Various biochemical pathways are connected to MMP regulation in the context of cancer pathophysiology, facilitating tumour invasion and migration. Among these pathways, the MAPK signalling pathway, including the JNK and ERK, mediates cell stress responses and promotes MMP expression in response to growth factors 11 , 30 . Similarly, the STAT3 pathway, activated by cytokines and growth factors, upregulates MMP-2 and MMP-9 expression, promoting ECM degradation, tumour invasion, and metastasis 31–33 . Exploring JNK, ERK, and STAT3, in particular, provides valuable insights into the upstream mechanisms of MMP regulation in cancer progression.

Exercise induces positive effects on a wide range of diseases, including cancer, neurodegenerative diseases, and mental health disorders by influencing muscle energy metabolism and improving overall health 34 , 35 . In cancer, exercise fortifies the immune system, reduces inflammation, and improves cellular metabolism while regulating molecular upstream and downstream pathways linked to cancer progression 36 . For instance, exercise activates AMPK, SIRT1, and PGC-1α to enhance energy efficiency and suppress cancer-promoting mechanisms 37 , 38 , while downregulating hyperactive pathways like PI3K/AKT/mTOR to reduce tumour growth and inflammation 39 . Furthermore, peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor delta (PPARδ), also activated by exercise, plays a key role in modulating the tumour microenvironment and lipid metabolism 40 . An important aspect of exercise benefits is MMP regulation; dysregulated MMP activity contributes significantly to cancer progression, and exercise has been shown to modulate MMP-2 and MMP-9 activity 41 . Collectively, these pathways illustrate how exercise affects cancer progression by targeting the underlying molecular mechanisms associated with cancer pathology 42 , that could directly and indirectly regulate MMP activity, inflammation, and cellular metabolism. However, for many people, especially those with cancer, heart disease, and other age-related illnesses, exercising may not always be possible or advisable. This has led to increased interest in exercise mimetics that produce the physiological effects of exercise without requiring physical activity, offering a potential alternative for harnessing the therapeutic effects of exercise 43 .

Exercise mimetics are a class of bioactive compounds designed to mimic the physiological and molecular effects of physical exercise without the need for actual physical activity 43 , 44 . However, unlike general bioactive compounds that exert biological effects through diverse and often isolated mechanisms, exercise mimetics are specifically defined by their ability to reproduce coordinated molecular and metabolic responses induced by physical exercise. Exercise mimetics primarily benefit health through three key mechanisms: (i) synthesising myokines, (ii) modulating signalling pathways such as AMPK, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, PPARδ and NF-κB, which regulate metabolism, inflammation, and cellular repair, and (iii) selectively influencing proteins, enzymes, or receptors involved in various cellular processes 45 . One of their therapeutic potential lies in their ability to influence signalling pathways similar to those activated during physical exercise, particularly those involved in energy metabolism in muscle, such as the AMPK, SIRT1, and PGC-1α pathways 44 , 46 . Moreover, exercise mimetics may also produce anti-metastatic effects by targeting MMP-2 and MMP-9. Since exercise mimetics could replicate the effect of real physical activities, they could create an unfavourable environment for cancer progression by simultaneously reducing inflammation and regulating MMP expression and activity 47 , 48 . Besides, multiple studies have demonstrated that the AMPK pathway is involved in regulating the invasion and migration of cancer cells by reducing the expression and enzymatic activity of MMP 49 , 50 . By reproducing the anti-inflammatory effects of exercise and regulating various signalling pathways, exercise mimetics might help foster an adverse environment for tumour development and metastasis 45 .

Based on the understanding that exercise influences MMP activity and multiple signalling pathways relevant to cancer progression, this study aimed to explore whether certain bioactive compounds with exercise-mimetic potential could replicate these effects by targeting MMPs. Here, we examined the six exercise mimetics, AICAR ( AIC ), Icariin ( Ica ), Berberine ( Ber ), Betaine ( Bet ), GW501516 ( GW ), and Metformin ( Met ), in regulating the activity of MMP-2 and MMP-9 through various methods ( Figure 1 ). Additionally, the expression levels of MMP-2 and MMP-9 and key signalling pathways involved in regulating those enzymes, such as MAPK and STAT3, in cancer cells in response to compound treatment were monitored. This approach allowed for a comprehensive assessment of the anti-metastatic effects of exercise mimetics by adjusting the expression of MMPs via regulating STAT3 signalling and systematically comparing the effects of multiple compounds, thereby opening new avenues for their application in cancer therapy.

sections.methods:
MMP-2/9 activity was assessed using gelatine zymography by detecting the degradation of gelatine. MMP-2 (80 nM; 72 kDa; Abcam, Cambridge, UK; Catalogue No. ab81550) and MMP-9 (0.2 nM; 92 kDa; R&D systems, USA; Catalogue No. 911-MP) were diluted in non-SDS sample buffer (containing 25% glycerol, 50 mM Tris, bromophenol blue). Exercise mimetics were dissolved in DMSO (with a final concentration of 1% DMSO) and incubated with MMP-2/9 with different concentrations ([MMP]:[exercise mimetics] = 1:0.01, 1:0.1, 1:1, 1:10, 1:100, 1:1000, and 1:10000) for 24 h with shaking (250 RPM) at room temperature. 18 μL of each solution was loaded into each gel lane.

The stacking gel comprised Tris-buffer (0.5 M, pH 6.8), 30% acrylamide, ddH 2 O, 10% SDS, 10% APS, and TEMED. The resolving gel (7.5% gelatine gel) contained Tris-buffer (1.5 M, pH 8.8), 30% acrylamide, ddH 2 O, 10% SDS, 10% APS, TEMED, and gelatine (4 mg/mL). Electrophoresis was conducted for 80–100 min (60 V for 60 min, followed by 80 V for 20–40 min). Subsequently, gels were washed twice with washing buffer (2.5% Triton X-100 solution) and incubated for 20 h with shaking (80 RPM) at 37 °C in developing buffer (50 mM Tris, pH 7.35, 0.02% NaN 3 , 50 μM CaCl 2 , 10 μM ZnCl 2 ). The gels were then stained with Coomassie Brilliant Blue (Bio-rad, Hercules, CA, USA) for 20 min and destained for 2 h. Clear bands appearing against the dark blue background represented regions of gelatine degradation, reflecting MMP enzymatic activity. Gel images were captured using a GelPic LED Box (Koreabiotech, Korea), and the intensity of each band was quantified using ImageJ.

Docking studies were performed according to previously published methods 93 . Flexible ligand docking studies for exercise mimetics against the apo-MMP-2 (PDB: 1CK7) and apo-MMP-9 (PDB: 1L6J) were conducted using AutoDock Vina 94 . The MMFF94 energy minimisation in Chem3D 16.0 was used to optimise the ligand structure for docking studies. The structural files of exercise mimetics and the enzymes were generated by AutoDock Tools and imported into PyRx 95 , which were used to run AutoDock Vina 94 . The search space dimensions were set to contain the entire peptide. The exhaustiveness of the docking runs was set to 1024. For each ligand, AutoDock Vina generated a set of poses ranked by binding affinity. The top-ranked binding pose (lowest binding energy) was selected and visualised using PyMOL.

Redocking validation was performed for six co-crystallized exercise mimetics. The docking protocol successfully reproduced the experimental poses with RMSD (lower bond) values ranging from 0.011 to 1.776 Å for MMP-2 and from 0.015 to 1.716 Å for MMP-9, all within the generally accepted threshold (< 2.0 Å), confirming the reliability of the docking approach ( Supporting Information Table S3 ). The search space for MMP-2 was centred at X = 59.19, Y = 96.39, Z = 146.86 Å, with dimensions of X = 83.88, Y = 67.61, Z = 75.21 Å, encompassing the catalytic site. For MMP-9, the grid box was centred at X = 36.87, Y = 38.85, Z = 34.63 Å, with dimensions of X = 48.36, Y = 78.61, Z = 66.45 Å.

The inhibitory activities of exercise mimetics were evaluated through the MMP-2 inhibitor screening assay colorimetric kit (Abcam, Cambridge, UK, Catalogue No. ab139446) following the manufacturer’s instructions. Before proceeding with the experiments, the enzyme, substrate, and exercise mimetics were diluted to an appropriate concentration in assay buffer and equilibrated to assay temperature at 37 °C. Assay buffer (70 μL), MMP-2 (20 μL) [concentration 3.28 U/μL], and exercise mimetics (1 μL) were added into each desired microplate well as ordered. The volume of each well was adjusted to 90 μL with the assay buffer. Then, the substrate (1 mM) was added to 10 μL. The absorbance (A412) was measured on a microplate reader (Ltek, Korea) ranging from 0 min to 300 min.

The relative activity of MMP-2 following treatment with each concentration of the exercise mimetics was calculated as follows: A i = V i V c

Where V i is the reaction rate of the sample treated with exercise mimetics, and Vc is the reaction rate of the control sample. The reaction rate for each sample was determined from the slope of the linear fit of absorbance versus incubation time.

K i value was determined through IC 50 as follows: K i = IC 50 1 + S K m where OriginPro calculated the IC 50 value, S is the substrate concentration, and Km is the Michaelis constant.

The human lung cancer cell line (A549) was purchased from the Korean Cell Line Bank (KLCB 10185, Seoul, Korea) and cultured in Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle Medium (DMEM; GIBCO, ThermoFisher Scientific, USA) culture medium supplemented with 10% foetal bovine serum (FBS, Welgene, South Korea), 2 mM L-glutamine (Sigma–Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA) and 100 units/ml Penicillin/streptomycin (Sigma–Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA). The cells were maintained in a humidified atmosphere at 37 °C in a 5% CO 2 incubator. This standardised culture medium and incubation environment provide optimal conditions for the robust growth and maintenance of the A549 cell line, ensuring their suitability for experimental use.

Our experiments were exclusively conducted in A549 lung cancer cells, a type of cancer cell known for its aggressive metastatic potential and high MMP expression. Besides, A549 cells are also widely recognised for their utility in studying MMP-related pathways and the metastatic process, making them an ideal model for exploring MMP-targeted therapies 96 .

Cells were seeded in a 96-well plate at a density of 2 × 10 4 cells per well in 100 μL of culture medium. Subsequently, the cells were treated with various concentrations of exercise mimetics, including AICAR , Icariin , Berberine , Betaine , GW501516 , and Metformin (TCI, Japan), ranging from 0 to 200 μM. After 24 h of incubation at 37 °C, 25 μL of MTT solution (5 mg/mL in phosphate-buffered saline, PBS, pH 7.4; GIBCO, ThermoFisher Scientific, USA) was added to each well, and the plates were further incubated for 4 h at 37 °C. Formazan produced by the cells was dissolved overnight at room temperature by the addition of a solubilisation buffer (100 μL) containing N, N-dimethylformamide (DMF; 50% v/v, aq.) and sodium dodecyl sulphate (SDS; 20% w/v). The absorbance (A590) was measured on a microplate reader (Ltek, Korea). Cell viability was determined relative to cells containing an equivalent amount of DMSO (1% v/v). Error bars were calculated as standard errors of three independent experiments.

The wound healing assay was performed to evaluate cancer cell migration. A549 cells were seeded in 24-well plates at a density of 1x10 5 cells per well and incubated at 37 °C in a humidified atmosphere with 5% CO 2 to allow for cell attachment and growth. Upon reaching approximately 90%-100% confluency, a scratch was made through the cell monolayer using a sterile 200 µL pipette tip to create a wound. The wells were washed with phosphate-buffered saline (1X PBS) to remove detached cells and debris. Then, the cells were treated with exercise mimetics at a concentration of 100 µM, with a final concentration of 1% DMSO. Immediately after treatment (0 h), images of the wounds were captured using a microscope (Nikon Eclipse TE2000U, 10X) equipped with a digital camera. Subsequent images were taken at 12 h and 24 h post-treatment. The wound areas were measured using ImageJ software. All experiments were performed in triplicate, and the data are presented as mean ± standard deviation (SD). The percentage of cell migration was calculated using the following equation: % Cell Migration = Initial Wound Area − Final Wound Area Initial Wound Area x 100 %

A549 cells (2 × 10 4 cells/well) were initially seeded in 96-well plates and allowed to attach for 24 h. Following attachment, the cells were transfected with MMP-2/9 plasmids using the Lipofectamine 3000 kit (ThermoFisher Scientific, USA) while concurrently treated with exercise mimetics at concentrations of 100 μM and 200 μM (with a final concentration of 1% DMSO). The transfection here was performed to achieve consistent and measurable overexpression of MMP-2/9, thereby minimising baseline variability and ensuring sufficient signal intensity for ICC/IF analysis. After 4–6 h of transfection, the medium was replaced to mitigate Lipofectamine-induced cytotoxicity, and exercise mimetics were continuously supplemented to the culture medium at the desired concentrations. The plates were then further incubated for 24 h for post-transfection and exercise mimetics treatment. MMP-2/9 plasmids were constructed by inserting the respective genes (MMP-2/CLH43A and MMP-9/CLG43B template DNAs, obtained from Sino Biological) into the pc3 bacterial expression vector, followed by recombinant synthesis using 5-alpha E. coli (New England Biolabs Inc.). Subsequently, the transfected cells underwent immunofluorescence staining procedures. The cell samples were pre-fixed by adding a volume of 4% paraformaldehyde for 15 min. Following fixation, the cells were washed with 1X PBS and then blocked for 1 h at room temperature using a blocking buffer consisting of 5% goat normal serum (Abcam, Cambridge, UK) and 0.3% Triton X-100 (Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA) in 1X PBS.

Then, the cell samples were incubated overnight at 4 °C with primary antibodies against MMP-2/9 (anti-MMP-2 antibody (ab97779) and anti-MMP-9 antibody (ab76003), both obtained from Abcam, Cambridge, UK at a dilution of 1:500). After washing with 1X PBS, the cells were incubated with fluorescent-conjugated secondary antibodies (goat anti-rabbit IgG H&L (ab150080), Abcam, Cambridge, UK) at a dilution of 1:500 for 2 h at room temperature. Immunofluorescence images were captured by using a fluorescence microscope (Nikon Eclipse TE2000U, 20X) with the Red-Texas filter set. The relative expression of MMP-2/9 was determined based on the fluorescence intensity of the stained cells, quantified using ImageJ.

Cells were collected at a density of 4 × 10 6 cells/petri dish after treatment with 1% DMSO and exercise mimetics (100 μM) for 24 h. Each group of cells was harvested and washed twice with PBS and protein lysed in 600 μL ice-cold lysis buffer (RIPA; ThermoFisher Scientific, USA) and incubated on ice for 30–45 min. Cell lysis was centrifuged at 20,000 × g for 20 min at 4 °C. The supernatant (15–25 μg of protein) was diluted in SDS-sample buffer (containing 40% glycerol, 25 mM Tris, 8% SDS, 5% mercaptoethanol, and 0,004% bromophenol blue). 20 μL of each sample was separated using a 10% Sodium Dodecyl Sulphate-Polyacrylamide Gel Electrophoresis, along with molecular weight markers (Bioneer, Korea). The gel was transferred to a nitrocellulose membrane (ThermoFisher Scientific, USA) and blocked overnight at 4 °C with a bovine serum albumin (BSA) solution (3% w/v, Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA) in Tris-buffered saline (TBS) containing 0.05%–0.1% Tween-20 (Sigma-Aldrich; TBS-T). The membrane was detected with MMP-2/9, JNK, phosphorylated JNK, ERK, phosphorylated ERK, and STAT3 antibodies overnight at 4 °C. Protein loading was estimated using Rabbit Polyclonal GAPDH antibody (anti-GAPDH-Loading control). The antibodies were purchased from Abcam (Cambridge, UK). Then, probed with Anti-Rabbit IgG (H + L), HRP conjugate secondary antibody (1:2500; Promega Corporation, USA) in 3% BSA in TBS-T solution for 1.5 h at room temperature. Blots were visualised using LAS-4000 Fujifilm (Fujifilm Corporation, Japan).

All experimental data are presented as mean ± standard deviation (SD) from at least three independent experiments. Statistical analyses were performed using Microsoft Excel. Comparisons between control and treatment groups were carried out using a two-tailed unpaired Student’s t- test. The control group was used as a reference for all comparisons. A p values of less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Significance levels are indicated as follows: p < 0.05 (*), p < 0.01 (**), and p < 0.001 (***).
sections.results:
Six compounds were selected from previously characterised exercise mimetics groups, based on their ability to replicate key physiological effects of physical exercise at the molecular level, making them promising alternatives or complementary therapies to physical activity, particularly in situations where physical activity may not be feasible. Physical exercise is known to induce a wide array of biochemical changes, such as the regulation of key signalling pathways involved in energy metabolism, inflammation, cellular survival, and tissue repair 51 , 52 . Notably, exercise intervention has been shown to modulate MMP levels, including MMP-2 and MMP-9, which are central to cancer cell invasion and metastasis 41 , 53–55 . Therefore, the selected exercise mimetics were hypothesised to inhibit cancer progression through MMP regulation.

First, AIC and Met , two established AMPK activators, were selected for their ability to mimic exercise-induced metabolic shifts, particularly in glucose uptake and fatty acid oxidation 56 . AMPK has been emerged as a promising target for cancer therapy because the activation of AMPK could reduce cancer cell growth in vitro and inhibit tumour development in vivo 57 , 58 . Therefore, the anti-cancer effects of AIC and Met are likely mediated through the functional activation of AMPK. A previous study demonstrated that AMPK activation by AIC suppresses the mTOR signalling pathway, leading to decreased cell proliferation and survival 59 . Similarly, Met -induced AMPK activation inhibits IGF-1-stimulated activation of the Akt/Tsc1/mTOR pathway, thereby reducing protein synthesis and slowing down cancer cell growth 60 .

In addition, Ica and Ber can activate AMPK, resulting in the improvement of glucose metabolism, reducing lipid accumulation, and enhancing mitochondrial function 61 , 62 . Ica and Ber are emerging candidate drugs for anti-cancer treatment with potent anti-proliferative effects against hepatocellular carcinoma, pancreatic cancer, and breast cancer 63–65 . Furthermore, they exhibit anti-inflammatory and anti-oxidant effects similar to the systemic reduction of inflammation and oxidative damage seen in regular exercisers 66 , 67 . By modulating PI3K/Akt and NF-κB pathways 67 , 68 , Ica and Ber may be able to help reduce chronic inflammation and inhibit cancer progression.

Besides, GW stands out for its role in activating PPARδ, a key regulator of fat metabolism and endurance adaptation during exercise 69 . PPARδ activation by GW can increase the activity of AMPK, and the increase in fatty acid oxidation in human skeletal muscle cells 70 . AMPK pathway not only mimics metabolic and cellular health benefits typically associated with exercise but also holds significance in cancer research. PPARδ was reported to repress inflammation-associated NF-κB and target genes 71 , which could lead to a reduction in MMP-2 and MMP-9 levels. In the context of cancer, it has been demonstrated that the activation of PPARδ by agonists including GW , could revert or inhibit tumorigenesis in colorectal, liver, skin, breast, testicular, pancreatic cancer, or neuroblastoma cells 72–75 . These effects suggest that GW could be a valuable candidate for cancer therapy, particularly through its ability to activate various biochemical pathways, reduce inflammation, and inhibit cancer progression.

Lastly, Bet has also been studied for its role in enhancing exercise performance by acting as an osmolyte, stabilising cellular function under stress 76 . Large amounts of Bet could be accumulated in cells without disrupting cell functions, while protecting cells, proteins, and enzymes under osmotic stress 77 . Through such effects, Bet helps maintain cellular homeostasis under stress, similar to how exercise induces adaptive stress responses that strengthen cellular resilience. Additionally, Bet has been known for its anti-inflammatory and anti-oxidant effects, critical in reducing cancer progression. It has been known for anti-inflammatory effects through its inhibition of the NF-κB signalling pathway and suppression genes such as TNF-α, VCAM-1, ICAM-1, iNOS, and COX-2 78 , 79 . Furthermore, Bet could block NF-κB by inhibiting two important activators MAPKs and NIK/IKK, resulting in the suppression of MMP expression and mitigating cancer cell invasion 78 .

Collectively, these six compounds have been reported in previous studies as exercise-mimetic agents because they activate key pathways normally stimulated by physical exercise. Their ability to reproduce metabolic, anti-inflammatory, and stress-adaptive responses supports their classification as exercise mimetics. Through these mechanisms, the selected exercise mimetics might also have anti-cancer ability, in part, by regulating the activity and/or expression of MMPs, particularly MMP-2 and MMP-9.

First, the effects of exercise mimetics on the activity of MMP-2 and MMP-9 were examined ( Figure 2 and Supporting Information Figure S1 ). The intensity of relative bands in the gels corresponds to the level of MMP activity in Figure 2 . Among the tested compounds, AIC appeared to moderately reduce MMP-2 activity to approximately 80% of the control, with greater than 10,000 equivalents ( Figure 2(A) ). Ica exhibited a more pronounced reduction, lowering MMP-2 activity to ca . 24% of the control at higher concentrations (greater than 10,000 equivalents; Figure 2(B) ). Notably, Ber demonstrated the strongest inhibitory effect on MMP-2 activity. It could reduce MMP-2’s enzymatic activity to less than 44% of the control with concentrations greater than 1,000 equivalents of Ber to MMP-2 ( Figure 2(C) ). This suggests that AIC , Ica , and Ber may interact with MMP-2 at key sites, such as the active or allosteric sites, and thereby potentially contribute to the downregulation of enzymatic activity.

Effect of (A) AICAR , (B) Icariin , (C) Berberine , (D) Betaine , (E) GW501516 , and (F) Metformin on the activity of MMP-2 by Zymography, respectively. Treatments were applied at concentration ratios ([MMP-2] : [exercise mimetics]) ranging from 1:0.01 to 1:10000 for 24 h. The data were presented as mean ± SD from three independent experiments.

Furthermore, effects of the exercise mimetics on MMP-2 activity were investigated kinetically ( Supporting Information Figure S1 ). Consistent with the zymography results, a decrease in the enzymatic activity was observed through colorimetric assay upon treatment of Ica and Ber , while AIC showed limited inhibition ( Supporting Information Figure S1 ; top row). Specifically, at the highest concentration of AIC (1 µM), a reduction in MMP-2 activity of approximately 20% was observed after 300 min. A greater reduction in the activity of MMP-2 was observed for Ica and Ber across concentrations ranging from 0.1 nM to 0.1 µM. The kinetic inhibitory constants ( K i ) for AIC , Ica , and Ber were determined to be 2.6 nM, 2.1 nM, and 2.2 nM, respectively. In contras t, Bet , GW , and Met displayed no significant inhibitory effect on MMP-2 activity in both zymography and colorimetric assays ( Figure 2(E and F) , and Supporting Information Figure S1 (E and F ). The lack of inhibition observed for these compounds suggests that they may not interact directly with the MMP-2 in a way that inhibits its activity or their mechanisms of action.

However, all exercise mimetics showed minimal effect on the activity of MMP-9 ( Supporting Information Figure S2 ). The relative band intensity in the zymography for MMP-9 remained between 95–100% of control levels, suggesting that all the compounds could not significantly impact the activity of MMP-9. This discrepancy may be due to structural differences between MMP-2 and MMP-9, which could result in less effective binding and stabilisation of the enzyme–exercise mimetics complex. Although the structures of both MMP-2 and MMP-9 are similar, subtle differences in the active site geometry and substrate-binding pockets may contribute to the stronger inhibitory effect of the exercise mimetics on MMP-2 compared to MMP-9. Additionally, the regulation of MMP-9 might involve different mechanisms compared to MMP-2, making it less susceptible to inhibition by the exercise mimetics.

To summarise, exercise mimetics, particularly AIC , Ica , and Ber , appeared to significantly inhibit MMP-2 activity, potentially suppressing cancer progression and metastasis by limiting extracellular matrix degradation. However, Bet , GW , and Met did not produce a notable effect on MMP-2 activity, possibly due to differences in their interactions with the enzyme or their mechanisms of action. Also, none of the exercise mimetics in this study affected MMP-9 activity.

AIC showed a less pronounced effect on MMP-2 activity, possibly due to weaker binding interactions with the enzyme compared to Ber and Ica . While Ica had a less potent effect on MMP-2 activity than Ber , this significant inhibition suggests that Ica can bind to MMP-2 and reduce its activity. Thus, the interactions between exercise mimetics and MMP-2 (PDB: 1CK7) have been investigated through docking simulations. AIC could interact with MMP-2 at the active site with a relatively strong binding energy (−8.6 kcal/mol), consistent with observed inhibition of MMP-2 activity in zymography and kinetic assays, indicating potential inhibitory effects ( Supporting Information Table S1 ). This interaction was mediated by the formation of multiple hydrogen bonds with residues ALA419, ALA422, THR426, THR428, ILE424, VAL400, and PRO423 ( Figure 3 ) involving the hydrogen (H) atoms from the -OH groups and the -NH groups, which could directly interfere with the substrate binding to MMP-2 and reduce its enzymatic activity.

Interaction between (A) AICAR , (B) Icariin , and (C) Berberine with the MMP-2 (PDB: 1CK7). Zn and Ca ions are represented as pink spheres and green spheres, respectively. The amino acid residues are involved in the diverse interactions; light green: hydrophobic interaction, green: hydrogen bond, pale pink: π–alkyl, pink: π–π stacking, purple: π–σ interactions.

In contrast, Ica and Ber may not bind to the active site. Instead, they interacted with the allosteric site, a regulatory region in the enzyme structure with strong binding energies of −10.5 kcal/mol and −9.2 kcal/mol, respectively ( Supporting Information Figure S3 ). Previous studies have shown that the binding of ligands, whether small or large, to an allosteric site can alter protein conformations and dynamics, thereby influencing binding events at distant functional sites 80 . Additionally, both Ica and Ber formed hydrogen bonds with residue HIS193, an amino acid located near the active site of MMP-2 that plays a crucial role in stabilising the catalytic Zn(II), thereby noncompetitively impairing enzymatic function ( Figure 3 ). These bonds involved hydrogen (H) atoms from the -OH groups in the Ica structure and oxygen (O) atoms from the 5-membered ring in the Ber structure. By interacting with the allosteric site, these compounds could induce conformational changes that potentially disrupt the enzyme’s catalytic function, thereby reducing its activity. This mechanism aligns with the experimental data showing reduced MMP-2 activity following treatment with Ica and Ber . Beyond hydrogen bonds, although Ica and Ber did not exhibit as many hydrogen bonds with MMP-2 as AIC did, they could still interact with the protein through π-interactions at the allosteric site ( Figure 3 ). In proteins, these π-interactions, such as π-π stacking or π-alkyl interactions, can stabilise the protein structure, promote protein-ligand interactions, and facilitate catalysis and self-assembly. 81 , 82 Thus, the interaction with Ica and Ber could potentially induce conformational changes in the protein, contributing to the inhibition of its enzymatic activity.

On the other hand, Bet and GW exhibited weak binding affinities and may not interact with the active or allosteric sites, correlating with their lack of effect on MMP-2 activity. Met , although it interacted with the active site, showed a weak binding energy of −6.6 kcal/mol, suggesting that the interaction was insufficient to significantly affect MMP-2 activity ( Supporting Information Figure S4 and Table S1 ). These findings underscore the importance of the intermolecular interactions in determining the inhibitory potential of exercise mimetics on MMP-2 activity, which appears to be contingent on both their binding affinity and binding location. AIC , Ica , and Ber , which bind strongly at either the active site or allosteric regions, could inhibit the catalytic activity of MMP-2 by either competitively hindering substrate binding or inducing conformation changes at the active site. In contrast, Bet , GW , and Met displayed limited inhibitory effects, likely due to their lack of significant interaction with these sites on MMP-2.

In addition, most of the tested compounds, including AIC , Ica , Ber , Bet , and GW , could not interact with either the active site or allosteric regions of MMP-9, while Met showed interactions at the active site but with relatively weak binding affinities, suggesting that they may not effectively inhibit MMP-9 activity ( Supporting Information Table S2 and Figure S5 ). This differential responsiveness may be explained by intrinsic structural distinctions between the two enzymes. Compared with MMP-2, MMP-9 appears to possess a more flexible and solvent-exposed catalytic pocket, with fewer amino acid residues available to form stabilising hydrogen bonds or π-interactions. Consequently, small molecules may bind less tightly or less persistently to MMP-9, resulting in weaker inhibition. This selectivity towards MMP-2 presents both advantages and limitations. Positively, it highlights the feasibility of developing MMP-2 specific inhibitors with reduced off-target activity. On the other hand, compounds that are effective against MMP-2 may not inhibit MMP-9 efficiently, which limits their broader applicability.

Taken together, the in silico data regarding MMP-ligand interactions in conjunction with the enzymatic inhibition experimental data indicate that compounds capable of binding to either the active site or allosteric regions of the enzyme with strong binding energies can substantially modulate the enzyme activity, potentially reducing the degradation of the extracellular matrix, an important process in cancer metastasis.

The MTT assay was performed to evaluate the viability of lung cancer (A549) cells treated with various exercise mimetics. Additionally, this assay was also conducted as a pre-emptive step to support the MMP expression data, ensuring that the compounds did not induce excessive cell death that could affect the interpretation of MMP expression results.

The cancer cells were exposed to a range of concentrations (10 to 200 µM) for 24 h ( Figure 4 ). Across the tested compounds, treatments with AIC , Bet , and Met did not significantly affect the viability of A549 cells within the same treatment period and concentration range. These compounds are known to be involved in metabolic processes within cells, influence mitochondrial function, reduce inflammation, and regulate signalling pathways. Thus, rather than directly killing cancer cells, their anti-cancer effects may manifest over longer treatment periods through indirect mechanisms. In contrast, Ica exhibited mild cytotoxicity, although only moderately in A549 cells, with over 80% of the cells remaining viable even at the maximum concentration of 200 µM. On the other hand, Ber and GW significantly reduced the viability of A549 cells in a dose-dependent manner, with viability dropping to <70% for A549 at 200 µM ( Figure 4 ). This indicates that Ica may have a less direct effect on cell viability compared to Ber and GW . Also, these concentration ranges of exercise mimetics were used in the following experiments.

The immunofluorescence method was applied to examine the effects of exercise mimetics on the expression of MMP-2 and MMP-9 in A549 cells ( Figures 5 and Supporting Information Figure S6 ). The A549 cells were treated with exercise mimetics at concentrations of 100 and 200 µM for 24 h. Under our experimental conditions, 100 µM treatment with AIC and Ica showed no significant effect on both MMP-2 and MMP-9 expression, while 200 µM treatment with AIC and Ica could reduce the amount of MMP-2 expression to 86% and 89%, and MMP-9 to 50% and 44% of the control, respectively. However, at 100 µM treatment, Ber , Bet , GW , and Met significantly reduced the expression of both MMP-2 and MMP-9. Specifically, Ber , Bet , GW , and Met downregulated MMP-2 expression to 34%, 81%, 23%, and 39% of the control, respectively ( Figure 5(A and C) ). Similarly, these compounds also reduced MMP-9 expression to 27% ( Ber ), 33% ( Bet ), 13% ( GW ), and 53% ( Met ) compared to the control ( Figure 5(B and D) ). These findings suggest that Ber , Bet, GW , and Met could directly downregulate MMP expression even at lower concentrations, while AIC and Ica require higher concentrations to inhibit the production of MMP-2/9. In line with these findings, wound healing assays revealed that several exercise mimetics also reduced A549 cell migration, with Ber and GW showing the most pronounced effects, followed by AIC , Ica , and Bet ( Supporting Information Figure S7 ). Met also demonstrated a reduction in migration, although its effect appeared weaker compared to the other compounds. Furthermore, when tested in HeLa cells, all compounds exhibited inhibition in both MMP-2 and MMP-9 expression, specifically Ber and GW at 50 µM, and AIC , Ica , Bet , and Met at 100 µM ( Supporting Information Figure S8 ).

In order to elucidate how exercise mimetics affect the expression of MMP-2 and MMP-9, an additional study was performed by investigating the protein expression level via Western Blot in A549 cells ( Figure 5(E and F) ). In alignment with the immunofluorescence results, treatment with exercise mimetics significantly reduced the expression of both MMP-2 and MMP-9 in A549 cells. At a concentration of 100 µM, all exercise mimetics demonstrated the ability to inhibit MMP-2 expression to varying extents. As shown in Figures 5(E and F) , AIC , Ica , Ber , Bet , and Met reduced MMP-2 levels to 51%, 38%, 25%, 40%, and 16% compared to control, respectively, with GW showing the least impact, decreasing MMP-2 expression to 73%. In terms of MMP-9, exercise mimetics at 100 µM also showed substantial inhibitory effects. AIC reduced MMP-9 expression to 52%, Ica to 35%, Ber to 16%, Bet to 64%, and Met to 34% of control levels ( Figure 5(E and F) ). GW , however, had minimal impact, reducing the expression of MMP-9 to 95%.

Since each method involves different processing steps, the accessibility of specific binding sites may differ, leading to varying signal intensities. For instance, the ICC/IF experiment enables the visualisation of specific proteins in the samples through the use of antibodies 83 , 84 . Thus, transfecting MMP-2/9 may lead to localised protein distribution within the cell, where GW can exhibit stronger inhibition. In contrast, Western blot measures total cellular protein levels, which may not reflect this localised inhibition as clearly 84 , 85 . These results reinforce the observation that AIC , Ica , Ber , Bet , and Met are particularly effective at targeting both MMPs, while GW appears to favour MMP-2 over MMP-9. The differential effectiveness of the mimetics may point to their varied mechanisms of action, possibly involving modulation of MMP transcription, signalling pathways such as AMPK, or other indirect regulatory mechanisms.

Many prior studies have shown that exercise mimetics influence pathways like AMPK or others and thus might indirectly regulate MMPs 49 , 50 . However, most studies have focused more generally on their role in metabolic health and inflammation. The effects on MMP-2 and MMP-9 specifically are less frequently reported, especially in relation to the direct inhibition of these MMPs in cancer cells. This current study provides detailed quantitative data showing significant downregulation of both MMP-2 and MMP-9, underscoring their potential as promising anti-cancer agents. Since MMPs facilitate tumour invasion and metastasis by degrading extracellular matrix components 13 . By reducing the expression of MMPs, exercise mimetics may suppress the invasive and metastatic capabilities of cancer cells. This inhibitory effect is likely related to the regulation of various signalling pathways involved in MMP transcription and activation.

MMP-2 and MMP-9 are known to be regulated by various key signalling pathways, such as JNK, ERK, and STAT3 via transcription. These pathways control the process of gene transcription and then lead to changes in MMP-2 and MMP-9 levels 31 . Therefore, to further investigate the underlying mechanism of the anti-cancer ability of exercise mimetics in A549 cells, Western blot assay was performed to detect changes in the expression of the MAPK (total and phosphorylated levels of JNK, ERK) and STAT3 pathways in response to the six selected exercise mimetics (100 µM) for 24 h ( Figure 6 ). At this concentration, almost all of the exercise mimetics, AIC , Ica , Bet , GW , and Met , did not significantly affect either the total or phosphorylated forms of JNK and ERK in A549 cells ( Figure 6 ). However, treatment with Ber slightly reduced total JNK levels to approximately 80% of the control, suggesting a partial inhibition of the JNK pathway by Ber . The lack of significant changes in MAPK signalling responses are highly context-dependent and may vary according to cell type, stimulus intensity, and experimental conditions. Therefore, it is possible that ERK and JNK pathways are not the primary mediators of exercise mimetic-induced MMP regulation in A549 cells under the conditions tested.

Despite the minimal impact on both JNK and ERK, these compounds exhibited a notable effect on the STAT3 signalling pathway. Ber , in particular, significantly inhibited the total form of STAT3, reducing its level to 4% of the control. This was followed by AIC , Ica , and Met , which reduced STAT3 levels to 17%, 18%, and 20%, respectively. Bet and GW showed a more moderate reduction, with STAT3 levels at 45% and 48% of the control, respectively. These findings suggest that exercise mimetics may primarily target the STAT3 pathway rather than the MAPK pathways in A549 cells. According to previous studies, AIC may also affect STAT3 indirectly through AMPK activation 86 . Ica , Ber , and Met have been extensively studied for their clear association with STAT3 inhibition 32 , 87 , 88 . Meanwhile, further research is needed to determine the direct relationship between Bet and GW with STAT3, as current studies are limited. This inhibition of STAT3 is noteworthy because STAT3 is a key transcription factor involved in promoting cancer cell proliferation, survival, and migration 33 , 89 . STAT3 has been shown to regulate the transcription of MMP-2 and MMP-9, driving extracellular matrix degradation and facilitating tumour cell invasion, making its inhibition a critical mechanism for controlling cancer progression 31 , 33 , 90 . By targeting MMP-2 and MMP-9, exercise mimetics can suppress their expression by inhibiting the STAT3 pathway.

Overall, our findings suggest that while exercise mimetics may not be potent inhibitors of the MAPK pathway in A549 cells, the greater inhibition of the STAT3 pathway highlights their potential for the development of therapeutic agents, particularly in cancers. The significant inhibition of STAT3 signalling by these mimetics could be attributed to their diverse bioactive properties, including anti-oxidant activity, anti-inflammatory effects, and their ability to modulate multiple cellular pathways. These characteristics could mimic the physiological benefits of physical exercise, which has been shown to suppress tumorigenesis through various mechanisms 36 . Additionally, although multiple exercise mimetics reduced MMP-2 activity and MMP-2/9 expression, most compounds showed no significant effects on the enzymatic activity of MMP-9. The inhibitory effects of exercise mimetics on MMP were also moderate compared to conventional MMP inhibitors (e.g., GM6001, marimastat), which have been known to typically exert direct catalytic inhibition in preclinical models 91 , 92 . Future studies should focus on validating these findings, testing additional cancer cell lines and other biological model, and investigating their potential to be used in combination therapies targeting multiple signalling pathways. Moreover, further experimental validation of the docking simulations, as well as additional structure-based studies using holo structures, site-directed mutagenesis, or competitive binding assays, should be conducted to understand the detailed mechanisms underlying the effects of exercise mimetics on regulating MMP activity and expression.
sections.conclusion: In conclusion, the impact of cancer underscores the urgent need for improved treatments, particularly those that can effectively inhibit metastasis. As key drivers of cancer cell invasion and spread, MMP-2 and MMP-9 become critical targets in the fight against cancer progression. This study highlights the potential of selected exercise mimetics, including AIC , Ica , Ber , Bet , GW , and Met , to modulate the activity and expression of MMP-2 and MMP-9. These compounds are not only known to replicate the terms of molecular and physiological benefits of exercise but also impact critical signalling pathways that are involved in the regulation of MMPs. Experimental findings indicated that exercise mimetics such as AIC , Ica , and Ber could effectively regulate MMP-2 activity by interacting with its active site or allosteric regions with strong binding energies. Furthermore, we demonstrated that exercise mimetics in this study could inhibit STAT3 pathways, but not JNK and ERK, effectively leading to MMP downregulation. Evidence supports exercise mimetics as a promising therapeutic agent potentially beneficial in early-phase cancers to prevent metastasis. Future research could establish these mimetics as a novel class of anti-metastatic anti-cancer agents, bringing the multifaceted benefits of exercise into accessible pharmacological treatments.
